scenes.title: Course Handbook and Study Guide
scenes.narration: Cardiac arrest is the only emergency in which the actions of the nearest person in the first three minutes matter more than everything done by everyone else afterwards. This course is built around that fact.

The course has eleven modules, issued as separate documents so departments can assign what each role needs. Modules 1 to 5 are the basic life support core, for every clinical staff member. Modules 6 to 11 carry the advanced life support, peri-arrest, post-arrest and systems content, for those who respond to or lead codes.

scenes.narration: The total course duration is 13 hours. About 9 of those are self-paced module study, 2.5 are applied practice and scenario work, and 1.5 are assessment. All of this is in addition to the hands-on provider course and skills assessment that certification requires. The hours are MedSkills' recommended durations, recorded automatically against each learner. Your hospital's resuscitation policy sets the certification and recertification interval, and that is binding.

This is a knowledge course. It builds understanding of resuscitation science, the algorithms and the hospital system around them, and it produces a MedSkills certificate of completion. It does not confer a provider card from the American Heart Association, the European Resuscitation Council or an equivalent body. Compressions, bag-mask ventilation and defibrillator operation are psychomotor skills, and they must be assessed physically at an authorised training centre. Use this course to prepare for and reinforce that training, not to replace it.

Each module carries a knowledge check, written in the style of the final assessment. The final assessment covers all eleven modules, and your institution sets the pass mark and the permitted attempts. On passing, you receive a verifiable MedSkills certificate of knowledge completion, with the date and duration written to your training record. The certificate records knowledge, not psychomotor skill, so your provider card must come from a hands-on course at a recognised training centre.

scenes.narration: The American Heart Association released the 2025 Guidelines on 22 October 2025, a comprehensive revision of the 2020 guidelines. If you trained on the 2020 guidelines, you are updating, not relearning. Most of what you know remains correct, starting with the compression rate of 100 to 120 per minute. The 30 to 2 ratio for single-rescuer adult cardiopulmonary resuscitation also holds, as do the reversible causes and the overall shape of the algorithms.

There is now a single unified Chain of Survival for adults and children, in or out of hospital. The term rescue breaths is retired: breaths now means assisted breathing, and ventilation is reserved for mechanical respiratory support. Opioid antagonists have entered the basic life support algorithm for healthcare professionals, and there is a new choking algorithm. In shockable rhythms, epinephrine now comes after initial defibrillation attempts have failed, not alongside them. Vasopressin is no longer recommended as a substitute for epinephrine. Each module notes where the 2025 position differs from 2020.

By the end you should recognise cardiac arrest within seconds and start compressions without waiting for permission. You should describe high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation precisely, and explain why each parameter matters. You should operate an automated external defibrillator and describe safe manual defibrillation. Then follow the adult cardiac arrest algorithm, work through the reversible causes systematically, assess a peri-arrest rhythm for instability, deliver the immediate bundle after return of spontaneous circulation, modify care in special circumstances, and function within a code team.

scenes.narration: Read the modules in order, because each builds on the previous one. Attempt every knowledge check before reading the answers. Print the algorithm figures and post them beside the resuscitation trolley. Bring this material to your hands-on provider course; the psychomotor training is far more effective when the reasoning is already in place. And practise: skills decay within months, and brief, frequent practice beats a long course every two years.

scenes.narration: This content is current as at August 2026 and is based on the 2025 Guidelines. Regional councils, including the European and Indian Resuscitation Councils, publish their own guidance, which may differ in detail. Drug doses, energy settings and targets must always be checked against your own hospital's resuscitation policy and your own device's recommended settings. Where your hospital protocol differs from this material, follow the hospital protocol and raise the discrepancy with your resuscitation committee.
